title: tk factory dashboard: a local TUI for watching the cloud factory
description:
Operator request (2026-08-20): mission control for the cloud factory, run in a local terminal — the counterpart to tk herd dashboard, which does this for a local herdr fleet.

Today the only cloud surfaces are tk cloud status (a flat list of run ids and states) and reading Workflow steps or R2 logs by hand, which is what the orchestrator has been doing all epic and it is not something to ask an operator to do.

Mirror internal/herd/dashboard (bubbletea) rather than inventing a second idiom: same keys, same fold behaviour, same read-only posture. What it shows:
- RUNS: id, project, epic, state, elapsed, cost so far (from gateway telemetry, never a self-report), and the lease holder.
- PHASE within a run: the Workflow step the run is on, boot attempt number, and the image digest it actually booted (see z1b — that digest being invisible cost several diagnosis cycles).
- HARNESS OUTPUT: tail the R2 segment stream live, which is the single most useful thing here — the operator currently cannot see what the agent is doing without hand-fetching R2 keys.
- GATES: pending questions with their epic and tick, and whether a phone or a terminal answered.
- REFUSALS: why a submission was refused (lease_held_by, budget_exhausted, awaiting_approval) from dispatch_log, so a factory that is declining work explains itself.

Two design constraints, both learned the hard way this epic:
1. READ-ONLY, and observability rather than authority. The board is not the completion authority; collect is. A dashboard that can stop or start runs invites acting on a stale view — if it ever gains actions, they route through the same closed command surface (D21) rather than a private path.
2. It must work when the factory is unreachable: show the last known state and say plainly that it is stale. An operator debugging a broken factory is exactly who needs this most.

Feed it from the run_event protocol, whose producers Phase 2 tick bne is adding — that protocol has existed with no consumers and this is its natural first one. Polling tk cloud status is the fallback when no stream is available, not the design.

You own the factory TUI. bmo owns tk cloud verbs; s7f owns the Workflow. bne just landed run_event producers, so consume those rather than polling — and the standard to beat is concrete: through this whole epic the operator had to keep asking whether a run was still alive, and the answer came from hand-written gateway scripts until l4l shipped tk cloud trace. A working run and a hung one must be distinguishable at a glance. tpl's keeper heartbeat is the shape that worked.

acceptance_criteria: tk factory dashboard shows live runs, their phase, streamed harness output, pending gates and refusal reasons from a local terminal against the deployed factory; it is read-only; it degrades to last-known state with an explicit staleness indicator when the factory is unreachable; it shares key bindings and fold behaviour with tk herd dashboard.
